messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Martin Ellis was 67, a school principal in a midsized American suburb, a husband of forty years, and by his own account a man who had once prided himself on being steady under pressure. That certainty was shaken on a winter evening when a pickup truck ran a red light and T-boned his sedan, spinning him into the median hard enough to make the airbags explode across his face and chest. In the seconds after impact he heard metal shrieking, shouted fragments from people outside, and the sudden slam of other cars braking nearby. The collision was life-threatening enough that, in the days afterward, the ordinary sight of cars hit by accident on the roadside, a burst of shouting, or any loud noise would seize him by the chest before he could reason with himself. Those moments did not just startle him; they pulled him straight back into the crash, and he would feel the terrifying scene coming over him again in flashes he could not shut off.

What Martin found most unsettling was that the memory would not stay in words. He could describe that he had been hit, but the frightening event never settled into a tidy story he could tell his wife or the therapist he finally saw. Instead it returned like a film, over and over, with the crushed hood, the violent jolt, and the helplessness of knowing he could not stop what was happening. At times, when he tried to think about it, he felt as if it were happening right now, not years ago, and that reliving left him with the conviction that he had been permanently changed for the worse. He also compared himself bitterly to other people he knew, certain somebody else would not have gotten into such a situation, and that thought deepened his sense that he had become a lesser version of himself.

From there, his days narrowed. Martin came to believe the world was a dangerous place and that danger could appear without warning, so he began watching for signs of it everywhere. If a hallway announcement at school lasted longer than expected, if a student was late to an appointment, or if a phone call dragged on without an answer, he assumed something bad was happening. The same dread spread into nights at home, where he could not relax even in his own living room, and sleep became broken and shallow. When he felt the alarm rising, he forced himself to think only positive thoughts, ate excessively to take the edge off, and told himself these were small disciplines that should help. In practice, they only gave him a brief sense of control; by pushing away the fear and filling himself with food, he became even more on guard for the next hint of trouble.

That vigilance did not calm him. Martin found himself scanning for shouting in the school building, flinching at loud noises from dropped books or slamming doors, and dreading any scene that reminded him of a crash. If he heard raised voices from the front office or saw a wreck on the morning commute, the old images came back with more force, and the return of those images confirmed his belief that the world was dangerous and that he was damaged. The more that happened, the more he avoided going to work unless absolutely necessary, rearranging meetings and stepping away from the building whenever he could. He was embarrassed by how often he checked the parking lot before crossing it and how tense he felt moving through normal routines, but he also felt he had no better option.

Over the following months, the cycle hardened. Each time Martin stayed home, skipped an unnecessary commitment, or swallowed his fear with another round of positive self-talk and food, he told himself he was managing. Yet the relief was short-lived, and the avoidance left him more isolated from the school he had led for years. It also fed the very beliefs that haunted him: if he could not cope with an ordinary workday, perhaps he really had been permanently altered; if a delayed text or a loud hallway noise could set off panic, perhaps he was right that danger was everywhere. His memories kept returning in vivid, wordless bursts, his body stayed keyed for the next threat, and the more he lived around those reactions, the more brittle his world became.

By the time Martin sought help, his wife had become concerned that he was disappearing into himself—sleeping poorly, eating too much in the evenings, and avoiding the school whenever possible. He came in because he was tired of living as though every delay were an omen and every sudden noise a warning, and because he feared he was losing the life he had built. What he hoped for, and what frightened him most, was the possibility that he might never again feel safe enough to stand in a classroom, hear a shout, or drive through an intersection without the crash rushing back.
